For most of its history Koh Samui was an island of fishing villages and coconut plantations, with Nathon as its port and Hainanese Chinese families among its traders. It had no roads until the early 1970s; backpackers began arriving in the 1970s, Bangkok Airways opened the airport in 1989, and the whole island became a single city municipality in 2012. Today about 70,000 people are registered residents, with many more living and working here.

How we wrote this: Samui's early history is thinly documented, and much of it rests on oral tradition. We mark how sure each date is in the timeline, and we present theories as theories.

Early settlement and the name

Bronze ritual drums found in Samui's southern hills suggest people lived here more than 2,000 years ago. Local tradition says the island was settled in around the 6th century by fishermen from the Malay Peninsula, and that traders from southern China stopped here on their way along the coast. From the 13th century, the island came within Siam's orbit and served as a waypoint for trade between China and India. A Chinese map from 1687 marks it as "Pulo Cornam".

Nobody knows for certain where the name "Samui" comes from. The main theories are:

  • A tree: a local tree called ton samui.
  • Hainanese: a word from the dialect of the Hainanese traders, for whom it was their first port of call in Siam.
  • Malay: the word saboey, meaning a safe haven.
  • Sanskrit or Tamil: a term connected with sea weather.

None of these has firm evidence behind it. "Koh" simply means island in Thai.

The coconut economy

For generations, coconuts were Samui's wealth. Hainanese settlers from the 19th century onwards planted coconut and cotton and shipped the produce to the mainland and on to Bangkok on traditional sailing boats. Most island families lived from coconut groves, fishing and small gardens, and the island was largely self-sufficient until the late 20th century.

Coconut palms still cover much of the lowland and the lower hills, and coconuts and rubber remain local products, though tourism has long overtaken both. The island's nickname, "the coconut island", comes from this era. Coconut still shapes Samui's food: the signature local dish, wai khua, is octopus cooked in coconut milk, and southern curries here lean on fresh coconut cream. See our restaurants guide for where to try them.

Visitors sometimes see trained monkeys picking coconuts on plantations. It is a traditional practice in southern Thailand, but it raises real animal-welfare concerns, and we don't recommend monkey shows.

Hainanese Chinese families and Nathon

Chinese immigrants, mostly Hainanese traders, arrived from the 19th century and became the island's merchants. They ran the shops, bought coconuts from the growers and owned many of the boats that carried them to market. Many of Samui's established business families today have Hainanese roots.

Nathon, on the west coast facing the mainland, grew as the port and administrative town. Its waterfront still has rows of old two-storey wooden and concrete shophouses, and the Hainan shrine in town is the centre of the community's festivals. At Chinese New Year, which falls on Saturday 6 February 2027, the most traditional rites on the island take place there, and Maenam's Chinese temple holds lion and dragon dances. Read our Nathon guide for a walking route past the old shophouses and the shrine.

Hua Thanon's Muslim fishing community

On the south-east coast, Hua Thanon is Samui's Muslim fishing village. Its colourful painted fishing boats, the morning fish market and the central mosque, built in 1984, give it a character quite different from the rest of the island. The 16 m bronze statue of the Chinese general Guan Yu, put up on the hill above the village in 2014 by islanders of Chinese descent, shows how closely Samui's communities live side by side. See Hua Thanon and the Guan Yu Shrine.

Buddhism on Samui

Most islanders are Theravada Buddhists, and every village has its temple (wat). A few stand out for their history:

  • Wat Samret in Na Mueang, a quiet village temple off the tourist trail.
  • Wat Khunaram, on the ring road in Na Mueang, keeps the mummified body of the monk Luang Pho Daeng, who died in the 1970s seated in meditation; his body sits in a glass case in the same posture. See Wat Khunaram.
  • Laem Sor Pagoda on the south coast, a coral-stone chedi dating from around 1907. See Laem Sor Pagoda.
  • The Big Buddha (Wat Phra Yai) on Koh Fan islet in the north-east, joined to Samui by a causeway; it has become the island's best-known landmark. See Big Buddha.
  • The Secret Buddha Garden in the central hills, a hillside sculpture garden that its creator began in 1976 and that opened to the public after his death in 1990. See Secret Buddha Garden.
  • Wat Plai Laem, built between 2004 and 2009, with its 18-armed white Guanyin on a lake platform, mixing Thai and Chinese Buddhist traditions. See Wat Plai Laem.

Wat Samret is said to be more than 150 years old. [check]

The temple calendar still shapes island life, from the candlelit processions of Makha Bucha to the Chak Phra festival, when temple floats are pulled through Nathon at the end of Buddhist Lent. Our temples guide covers every major temple and its etiquette.

The ring road and the first tourists

Until the early 1970s Samui had no roads at all. Villages were linked by footpaths and by boat, and crossing the island's 15 km width could take a whole day. The first roads, which grew into today's 51 km ring road, transformed island life: coconuts could reach the piers faster, and the island became easier to explore.

At about the same time, the first Western backpackers found their way to Samui, travelling by boat from the mainland and staying in simple rooms with local families. Sociologists who studied the island describe modern tourism picking up pace in the late 1970s. Simple beach bungalows sprang up, with development starting at Chaweng, and by the 1980s Samui was on the map as Bangkok, Pattaya and Phuket became mass-market destinations. In 1985 the Tourism Authority of Thailand launched a master plan for the area.

Early travellers often reached the island on the same cargo boats that carried coconuts to the mainland. [check]

Chaweng grew fastest, from a quiet bay to the island's busiest beach; see Chaweng.

The airport

Bangkok Airways built Samui's airport itself and opened it in 1989. It is still privately owned and run by the airline, which explains its distinctive open-air terminal, tropical gardens and the airline's near-monopoly on flights. The airport turned Samui from a long overland journey into a one-hour hop from Bangkok, and mass tourism grew through the 1990s.

A major expansion is planned: capacity is to rise to 6 million passengers a year, with boarding gates increased from 7 to 11. A March 2026 update put the start of construction in the second quarter of 2026 and completion in 2030. More on today's flights: Koh Samui airport.

Local government

Samui is a district (amphoe) of Surat Thani province, divided into 7 subdistricts: Ang Thong (including Nathon), Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam, Na Mueang, Maret (Lamai), Bo Phut (Chaweng, Bophut, Bangrak and Choeng Mon) and Mae Nam. Its local government developed step by step:

YearStatus
1956Sanitary district around the main settlement
1963Sanitary district enlarged to cover Samui and Phangan
1973Phangan becomes a separate sanitary district
1981The sanitary district covers the whole of Samui district
1999Subdistrict municipality
2008Town municipality
2012City municipality (Thesaban Nakhon Ko Samui) covering the whole island

Because the municipality covers the whole island, Samui has one mayor and one city council for everything from rubbish collection to building permits, while national matters such as immigration, land registration and policing are run by central government offices on the island. Island facts and figures: Koh Samui facts.

Storms

Samui's weather follows the north-east monsoon, with its heaviest rain from October to December. Tropical storms are rare but memorable. In early January 2019, Tropical Storm Pabuk crossed the Gulf of Thailand, stopping ferries to the islands and closing Ang Thong Marine Park for several days, and many visitors were stranded until the sea calmed. Today's forecasts: Koh Samui weather.

Samui, Phangan and the islands around them

Samui has always been the hub of an archipelago. For a decade its local government covered Koh Phangan too: the sanitary district created in 1956 was enlarged to include Samui and Phangan in 1963, and Phangan became a separate district in 1973. Fishing families moved between the islands, and the boats that carried coconuts to the mainland called at both.

To the west lies the Ang Thong archipelago of 42 islands, now a national marine park. The park protects limestone islands, a green inland lake and coral reefs, and it closes every year from 1 November to 15 December for the monsoon. The southern islets of Koh Madsum and Koh Tan, a short boat ride from Thong Krut, are home to small communities and Samui's famous swimming pigs. Our islands near Koh Samui guide and the sister site angthongmarinepark.com tell their stories.

Samui today

Koh Samui is Thailand's second-largest island after Phuket, at about 229 km². Its registered population is about 70,000 (70,059 in 2019), though many more people live and work here without being registered as residents. Tourism is the island's economy, with coconut and rubber now minor products.

  • The White Lotus effect: season 3 of the HBO series, filmed largely at a resort on the north-west coast and aired from February to April 2025, brought a wave of new interest, and foreign bookings for Songkran 2025 rose sharply.
  • Protecting the hills: new environmental rules took effect in May 2025, limiting building on steep slopes and high ground, and authorities have since raided illegal hillside villas and forest encroachment.
  • Visas: from 15 September 2026, visa-free stays for most Western visitors were cut from 60 to 30 days.
  • The airport: expansion to 11 gates and 6 million passengers a year is planned for 2030.

Much of old Samui is still there if you look for it: Nathon's shophouses, Hua Thanon's boats, village temples and coconut groves on the back roads. The Jungle Discovery jeep safari (1,500 THB adult) visits Wat Khunaram, Na Muang waterfall and the Secret Buddha Garden in a day. The islands offshore have their own story: Ang Thong Marine Park, protected as a national park, reopens on 16 December after its 1 November–15 December closure (the Ang Thong speedboat day tour costs 1,800 THB adult), and the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult) runs all year. For customs and festivals, read our Thai culture and traditions guide.
